<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" /></noinclude>the linear factor which occurs to the second power in <math>f</math>. If, moreover, <math>\Delta</math> vanishes identically <math>f</math> is a perfect cube.

''The Binary Quartic''.—The fundamental system consists of five forms <math>a^4_x=f</math>; <math>(f,f')^2=(ab)^2a^2_xb^2_x=\Delta^4_x</math>; <math>(f,f')^4=(ab)^4=i</math>; <math>(f,\ \Delta)^1=(a\Delta)a^3_x\Delta^3_x=(ab)^2(cb)a^2_xb_xc^3_x=t</math>; <math>(f,\Delta)^4=(a\Delta)^4=(ab)^2(bc)^2(ca)^2=j</math>, viz. two invariants, two quartics and a sextic. They are connected by the relation
{{block center|<math>2t^2=\frac{1}{2}if^2\Delta-\Delta^3-\frac{1}{3}jf^3.</math>}}
The discriminant, whose vanishing is the condition that <math>f</math> may possess two equal roots, has the expression <math>j^2-\frac{1}{6}i^3</math>; it is nine times the discriminant of the cubic resolvent <math>k^3-\frac{1}{2}ik-\frac{1}{3}j</math>, and has also the expression <math>4(t,t')^6</math>. The quartic has four equal roots, that is to say, is a perfect fourth power, when the Hessian vanishes identically; and conversely. This can be verified by equating to zero the five coefficients of the Hessian <math>(ab)^2a^2_xb^2_x</math>. Gordan has also shown that the vanishing of the Hessian of the binary <math>n^{ic}</math> is the necessary and sufficient condition to ensure the form being a perfect <math>n^{th}</math> power. The vanishing of the invariants <math>i</math> and <math>j</math> is the necessary and sufficient condition to ensure the quartic having three equal roots. On the one hand, assuming the quartic to have the form <math>4x^3_1x_2</math>, we find <math>i=j=0</math>, and on the other hand, assuming <math>i=j=0</math>, we find that the quartic must have the form <math>a_0x^4_1+4a_1x^3_1x_2</math> which proves the proposition. The quartic will have two pairs of equal roots, that is, will be a perfect square, if it and its Hessian merely differ by a numerical factor. For it is easy to establish the formula <math>(yx)^2\Delta^4_x=2f.f^2_y-2(f^1_y)^2</math> connecting the Hessian with the quartic and its first and second polars; now <math>\alpha</math>, a root of <math>f</math>, is also a root of <math>\Delta^4_x</math>, and consequently the first polar <math>f^1_y = y_1\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} + y_2\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}</math> must also vanish for the root <math>\alpha</math>, and thence <math>\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}</math> and <math>\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}</math> must also vanish for the same root; which proves that <math>\alpha</math> is a double root of <math>f</math>, and <math>f</math> therefore a perfect square. When <math>f = 6x^2_1x^2_2</math> it will be found that <math>\Delta = -f</math>. The simplest form to which the quartic is in general reducible is <math>f = x^4_1 + 6mx^2_1x^2_2 + x^4_2</math>, involving one parameter <math>m</math>; then <math>\Delta^4_x = 2m(x^4_1 + x^4_2) + 2(1 - 3m^2)x^2_1x^2_2</math>; <math>i = 2(1 + 3m^2)</math>; <math>j = 6m(1 - m)^2</math>; <math>t = (1 - 9m^2)(x^2_1 - x^2_2)(x^2_1 + x^2_2)x_1x_2</math>. The sextic covariant <math>t</math> is seen to be factorizable into three quadratic factors <math>\phi = x_1x_2</math>, <math>\psi = x^2_1 + x^2_2</math>, <math>\psi = x^2_1 - x^2_2</math>, which are such that the three mutual second transvectants vanish identically; they are for this reason termed conjugate quadratic factors. It is on a consideration of these factors of <math>t</math> that Cayley bases his solution of the quartic equation. For, since <math>-2t^2 = \Delta^3 - \frac{1}{2}if^2\Delta - \frac{1}{3}j(-f)^3</math>, he compares the right-hand side with the cubic resolvent <math>k^3 - \frac{1}{2}i\lambda^2k - \frac{1}{3}j\lambda^3</math>, of <math>f = 0</math>, and notices that they become identical on substituting <math>\Delta</math> for <math>k</math>, and <math>-f</math> for <math>\lambda</math>; hence, if <math>k_1</math>, <math>k_2</math>, <math>k_3</math> be the roots of the resolvent
{{block center|<math>-2t^2 = (\Delta + k_1f)(\Delta + k_2f)(\Delta + k_3f)</math>;}}
and now, if all the roots of <math>f</math> be different, so also are those of the resolvent, since the latter, and <math>f</math>, have practically the same discriminant; consequently each of the three factors, of <math>-2t^2</math>, must be perfect squares and taking the square root
{{block center|<math>t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{-2}}\phi.\chi.\psi</math>;}} and it can be shown that <math>\phi</math>, <math>\chi</math>, <math>\psi</math> are the three conjugate quadratic factors of <math>t</math> above mentioned. We have <math>\Delta+k_1f=\phi^2</math>, <math>\Delta+k_2f=\chi^2</math>, <math>\Delta+k_3f=\psi^2</math>, and Cayley shows that a root of the quartic can be expressed in the determinant form

{{block center|<math>\begin{vmatrix} 1, & k_1, & \phi^1_y \\ 1, & k_2, & \chi^1_y \\ 1, & k_3, & \psi^1_y \end{vmatrix}</math>}}

{{block center|<math>y_1=0</math>}}

{{block center|<math>y_2=1</math>}}

the remaining roots being obtained by varying the signs which occur in the radicals <math>\phi^1_y</math>, <math>\chi^1_y</math>, <math>\psi^1_y</math>. The transformation to the normal form reduces the quartic to a quadratic. The new variables are the linear factors of <math>\phi</math>. If <math>\phi=r_x.s_x</math>, the normal form of <math>a^4_x</math>, can be shown to be given by
{{block center|<math>(rs)^4.a^4_x=(ar)^4s^4_x+6(ar)^2(as)^2r^2_xs^2_x+(as)^4r^4_x</math>;}}
<math>\phi</math> is any one of the conjugate quadratic factors of <math>t</math>, so that, in determining <math>r_x</math>, <math>s_x</math> from <math>\sqrt{\Delta+k_1f}=0</math>, <math>k_1</math> is any root of the resolvent. The transformation to the normal form, by the solution of a cubic and a quadratic, therefore, supplies a solution of the quartic. If <math>(\lambda\mu)</math> is the modulus of the transformation by which <math>a^4_x</math> is reduced to the normal form, <math>i</math> becomes <math>(\lambda\mu)^4i</math>, and <math>j</math>, <math>(\lambda\mu)^3j</math>; hence <math>\frac{i^3}{j^3}</math> is absolutely unaltered by transformation, and is termed the absolute invariant. Since therefore <math>\frac{i^3}{j^2}=\frac{2}{9}\,\frac{(1+3m^2)^2}{m^2(1-m^2)^2}</math> we have a cubic equation for determining <math>m^2</math> as a function of the absolute invariant.

''Remark''.—Hermite has shown (''Crelle'', Bd. lii.) that the substitution, <math>z = \frac{i}{j}\,\frac{\Delta}{f}</math>, reduces <math>\frac{x_2\partial x_1 - x_1\partial x_2}{\sqrt{j}}</math> to the form
{{block center|<math>\frac{1}{2i}\sqrt{-\frac{j}{2}}\,\frac{\partial z}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2}z+\frac{j^2}{i^3}z^3}}.</math>}}

''The Binary Quintic''.—The complete system consists of 23 forms, of which the simplest are <math>f = a^5_x</math>; the Hessian <math>\text{H} = (f,f')^2 = (ab)^2a^3_xb^3_x</math>; the quadratic covariant <math>i = (f,f')^4 = (ab)^4a_xb_x</math>; and the nonic covariant <math>\text{T} = (f,(f',f'')^2)^1 = (f,\text{H})^1 = (a\text{H})a^4_x\text{H}^5_x = (ab)^2(ca)a^2_xb^3_xc^4_x</math>; the remaining 19 are expressible as transvectants of compounds of these four.

There are four invariants <math>(i,i')^2</math>; <math>(i^3,\text{H})^6</math>; <math>(f^2,i^5)^{10}</math>; <math>(fl,i^7)^{14}</math>

four linear forms <math>(f,i^2)^4</math>; <math>(f,i^3)^5</math>; <math>(i^4,\text{T})^8</math>; <math>(i^5,\text{T})^9</math>

three quadratic forms <math>i</math>; <math>(\text{H},i^2)^4</math>; <math>(\text{H},i^3)^5</math>

three cubic forms <math>(f,i)^2</math>; <math>(f,i^2)^3</math>; <math>(i^3,\text{T})^6</math>

two quartic forms <math>(\text{H},i)^2</math>; <math>(\text{H},i^2)^3</math>.

three quintic forms <math>f</math>; <math>(f,i)^1</math>; <math>(i^2,\text{T})^4</math>

two sextic forms <math>\text{H}</math>; <math>(\text{H},i)^1</math>

one septic form <math>(i,\text{T})^2</math>

one nonic form <math>\text{T}</math>. We will write the cubic covariant <math>(f, i)^2 = j</math>, and then remark that the result, <math>(f, j)^3 = 0</math>, can be readily established. The form <math>j</math> is completely defined by the relation <math>(f, j)^3 = 0</math> as no other covariant possesses this property.

Certain convariants of the quintic involve the same determinant factors as appeared in the system of the quartic; these are <math>f</math>, <math>\text{H}</math>, <math>i</math>, <math>\text{T}</math> and <math>j</math>, and are of special importance. Further, it is convenient to have before us two other quadratic covariants, viz. <math>\tau = (j, j)^2 j_x j_x</math>; <math>\theta = (i\tau)i_x\tau_x</math>; four other linear covariants, viz. <math>\alpha = -(ji)^2 j_x</math>; <math>\beta = (i\alpha)i_x</math>; <math>\gamma = (\tau\alpha)\tau_x</math>: <math>\delta = (\tau\beta)\tau_x</math>. Further, in the case of invariants, we write <math>\text{A} = (i, i')^2</math> and take three new forms <math>\text{B} = (i, \tau)^2</math>; <math>\text{C} = (\tau, \tau')^2</math>; <math>\text{R} = (\beta\gamma)</math>. Hermite expresses the quintic in a ''forme-type'' in which the constants are invariants and the variables linear covariants. If <math>\alpha</math>, <math>\beta</math> be the linear forms, above defined, he raises the identity <math>a_x(\alpha\beta) = \alpha_x(a\beta) - \beta_x(a\alpha)</math> to the fifth power (and in general to the power <math>n</math>) obtaining
{{block center|<math>(\alpha\beta)^5 f = (a\beta)^5 \alpha^5_x - 5(a\beta)^4 (a\alpha) \alpha^4_x \beta_x + \dots - (a\alpha)^5 \beta^5_x</math>;}}
and then expresses the coefficients, on the right, in terms of the fundamental invariants. On this principle the covariant <math>j</math> is expressible in the form
{{block center|<math>\text{R}^2 j = \delta^3 + \frac{3}{2}\text{B}\delta^2\alpha + \frac{3}{4}\text{AC}\delta\alpha^2 + \frac{3}{8}\text{C}(3\text{AB} - 4\text{C})\alpha^3</math>}}
when <math>\delta</math>, <math>\alpha</math> are the above defined linear forms.

Hence, solving the cubic,
{{block center|<math>\text{R}^2 j = (\delta - m_1\alpha)(\delta - m_2\alpha)(\delta - m_3\alpha)</math>}}
wherein <math>m_1</math> <math>m_2</math>, <math>m_3</math> are invariants.

Sylvester showed that the quintic might, in general, be expressed as the sum of three fifth powers, viz. in the canonical form <math>f = k_1(p_x)^5 + k_2(q_x)^5 + k_3(r_x)^5</math>. Now, evidently, the third transvectant of <math>f</math>, expressed in this form, with the cubic <math>p_xq_xr_x</math> is zero, and hence from a property of the covariant <math>j</math> we must have <math>j = p_xq_xr_x</math>; showing that the linear forms involved are the linear factors of <math>j</math>. We may therefore write
{{block center|<math>f = k_1(\delta - m_1\alpha)^5 + k_2(\delta - m_2\alpha)^5 + k_3(\delta - m_3\alpha)^5</math>;}}
and we have merely to determine the constants <math>k_1</math>, <math>k_2</math>, <math>k_3</math>. To determine them notice that <math>\text{R} = (\alpha\delta)</math> and then
{{block center|<math>(f, \alpha^5)^5 \ = -\text{R}^5(k_1 + k_2 + k_3)</math>,}}
{{block center|<math>(f, \alpha^4\delta)^5 = -5\text{R}^5(m_1k_1 + m_2k_2 + m_3k_3)</math>,}}
{{block center|<math>(f, \alpha^3\delta^2)^5 = -10\text{R}^5(m^2_1k_1 + m^2_2k_2 + m^2_3k_3)</math>,}}
three equations for determining <math>k_1</math>, <math>k_2</math>, <math>k_3</math>. This canonical form depends upon <math>j</math> having three unequal linear factors. When <math>\text{C}</math> vanishes <math>j</math> has the form <math>j = p^2_xq_x</math>, and <math>(f, j)^3 = (ap)^2(aq)a^2_x = 0</math>. Hence, from the identity <math>a_x(pq) = p_x(aq) - q_x(ap)</math>, we obtain <math>(pq)^5f = (aq)^5p^5_x - 5(ap)(aq)^4p^4_xq_x - (ap)^5q^5_x</math>, the required canonical form. Now, when <math>\text{C} = 0</math>, clearly (see ''ante'') <math>\text{R}^2j = \delta^2\rho</math> where <math>\rho = \delta + \frac{3}{2}\text{B}\alpha</math>; and Gordan then proves the relation
{{block center|<math>6\text{R}^4.f = \text{B}\delta^5 + 5\text{B}\delta^4\rho - 4\text{A}^2\rho^5</math>,}}
which is Bring's form of quintic at which we can always arrive, by linear transformation, whenever the invariant <math>\text{C}</math> vanishes.

''Remark.''—The invariant <math>\text{C}</math> is a numerical multiple of the resultant of the covariants <math>i</math> and <math>j</math>, and if <math>\text{C} = 0</math>, <math>\rho</math> is the common factor of <math>i</math> and <math>j</math>.

The discriminant is the resultant of <math>\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}</math> and <math>\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}</math> and of degree 8 in the coefficients; since it is a rational and integral function of the fundamental invariants it is expressible as a linear function of <math>\text{A}^2</math> and <math>\text{B}</math>; it is independent of <math>\text{C}</math>, and is therefore unaltered when <math>\text{C}</math> vanishes; we may therefore take <math>f</math> in the canonical form
{{block center|<math>6\text{R}^4f = \text{B}\delta^5 + 5\text{B}\delta^4\rho - 4\text{A}^2\rho^5.</math>}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
